title: The Spanish-American War and the Question of Empire, 1898

documents.citation: President William McKinley, War Message to Congress, April 11, 1898 — Bryan, William Jennings, ed., Republic or Empire (1899), public domain, public domain
documents.excerpt: The present condition of affairs in Cuba is a constant menace to our peace and entails upon this Government an enormous expense. With such a conflict waged for years in an island so near our border and with which our people have such trade and business relations; when the lives and liberty of our citizens are in constant danger and their property destroyed and themselves ruined; where our trading vessels are liable to seizure and are seized at our very door by warships of a foreign nation — the expedient of enforcing American interests will justify forceful intervention.

documents.citation: Teller Amendment, April 20, 1898, Bryan, William Jennings, ed., Republic or Empire (1899), public domain — public domain
documents.excerpt: Resolved by the Senate and House of Representatives... That the United States hereby disclaims any disposition or intention to exercise sovereignty, jurisdiction, or control over said Island except for the pacification thereof, and asserts its determination, when that is accomplished, to leave the government and control of the Island to its people.

documents.citation: Platt Amendment, 1901, Statutes at Large of the United States — public domain
documents.excerpt: The government of Cuba consents that the United States may exercise the right to intervene for the preservation of Cuban independence, the maintenance of a government adequate for protecting life, property, and individual liberty, and for discharging the obligations with respect to Cuba imposed by the Treaty of Paris on the United States... Cuba will sell or lease to the United States lands necessary for coaling or naval stations at certain specified points to be agreed upon with the President of the United States.
